vignette:
Fatima is a 68-year-old married woman of Lebanese descent who has worked as a correctional officer at a medium-security state prison for nearly two decades. She was referred for psychological assessment following a period of escalating distress that her husband described as having "changed her completely." Her PCL-5 score of 35 places her above the threshold for probable PTSD, and her presentation is consistent with a chronic, self-reinforcing pattern rooted in an assault she experienced approximately fourteen months ago.

The incident occurred during what began as a routine cell inspection. An incarcerated individual, whom Fatima had worked alongside other officers to manage for years, attacked her without warning in a corridor she believed was adequately monitored. He struck her from behind, and she was on the floor before she had any conscious awareness of what was happening. What haunts her most is not the physical pain but the silence that preceded it - the particular hush of an empty hallway that she had never before registered as dangerous. A younger colleague was stationed nearby and did not intervene quickly enough. Fatima has never fully forgiven him, and she has never fully forgiven herself. She had been the senior officer on that corridor. She believed, and continues to believe, that it was her responsibility to have anticipated what happened and to have protected those under her watch.

In the months that followed, Fatima found herself unable to trust that silence meant safety. At work - where she has remained, partly out of financial necessity and partly because she refuses to let the assault define her - she scans every corridor, every doorway, every cluster of inmates, reading the environment for signs of what might come next. Her body often responds before her mind catches up: she has startled violently at a door closing, at a colleague appearing in her peripheral vision, at the particular quality of quiet that settles over a cellblock before count. These threat responses have deepened her conviction that the world is fundamentally dangerous and that people - colleagues, inmates, even strangers - cannot be trusted to behave predictably or safely. She has come to see herself as permanently marked by what happened, permanently outside the easy confidence that others seem to carry, an outsider even among the officers she has worked beside for years.

These appraisals - that she failed, that she is now different, that trust is no longer available to her - have driven Fatima toward a set of strategies that feel, to her, like the only rational response. She keeps herself surrounded by people at almost all times, filling her off-hours with family visits, neighbourhood gatherings, and phone calls, so that she is never left alone with the thoughts that crowd in when the house goes quiet. She has quietly dropped several responsibilities that once anchored her sense of competence: she no longer takes the lead during shift briefings, has declined a supervisory role she was offered, and has stopped driving the route that passes the facility entrance on her days off. These withdrawals, though they offer short-term relief, have progressively narrowed her world and reinforced her belief that she is no longer capable - that she failed once and will fail again. The constant socialising, meanwhile, keeps her in a state of low-grade vigilance even in ostensibly safe settings; surrounded by people she cannot fully trust, she finds herself scanning rooms, tracking exits, monitoring faces, so that the very strategy meant to soothe her threat system keeps it activated.

The hypervigilance itself has begun to feed back into her appraisals. Because her body reacts before her mind can intervene, she interprets each startle, each racing heart, each sleepless night as further evidence that something is genuinely wrong - with the world, and with her. She cannot sleep soundly. She lies awake listening for sounds she cannot name, and the silence between them feels like the silence in that corridor. What finally brought Fatima to seek help was a conversation with her husband, who told her quietly that he was frightened - not of anything external, but of losing her to whatever she had become. What she most hopes for, she said at intake, is to stop feeling like a stranger in her own life. What she most fears is that it may already be too late.
